Standalone stage

Demo-to-Sim test

Four research agents, one per task, reconstruct the human demonstration, write their own verification criteria, build a training simulator with a free wrist, train a policy with reinforcement learning and verify it themselves — with no target environment and no official success criteria. Everything below is what the agents recorded, in the order received; it is their own account, not an official evaluation.

Documents the agents receive: Demo-to-Sim documentation (every bundle, and which run received it).

r0003 · criteria v1Nov 03, 01:34 EST

  • 7372 characters of criteria text
Criteria text

Agent's verification criteria, version 1

These are my own simulation claims, not an official evaluation. Source: TASK.md, the 315-frame 30 fps demonstration, and reconstruction version 1. They are recorded before training or judging a policy. All conditions below must pass in order in one uninterrupted episode. Ten fixed evaluation seeds (1000–1009) will be used; report every episode and require at least 9/10 complete successes, including nominal seed 1000. No criterion is relaxed in response to policy performance.

Evidence and uncertainty

Dense video inspection: release boundaries at frames 52, 163, 199 and capture at 67, 178, 216, with approximately one frame boundary uncertainty. Flight durations are approximately 0.50, 0.50, 0.567 seconds. Known-radius, gravity-constrained reconstruction gives rises from first unambiguously airborne sample of 0.215, 0.247, 0.299 m; horizontal ranges no more than 0.04 m. These are estimates, not calibrated ground truth: focal/depth ambiguity, partial occlusion, and motion blur remain. Gravity was constrained during fitting. The right wrist travels through a total 0.226 m vertical range and 0.117 m forward range; lateral range 0.036 m. Reconstructed anatomical palm normal tilt to vertical is median 21.0°, p95 43.8°. Wrist reconstruction is supported on 312/315 frames.

The sphere in the task specification is unmarked. Exact demonstrated spin angles and directions cannot be recovered, and the reference stores no invented rotations. Visible thumb/finger regrasping and TASK.md establish the three spin stages. For a definite interpretation of “spin,” I require one full directional turn in each stage. This is an explicit instruction-based assumption, not a measured video angle.

Ordered task conditions

  1. Initial support. Start palm up with the tennis ball supported by actual robot contact, at the demonstration's initial held position after fixed anatomical retargeting. Settle 0.20 s before task time begins. No attachment, artificial ball force or pose reset is permitted after settling.
  2. Toss and catch 1. One contact-free ballistic flight with release within 1.733 ± 0.25 s, capture within 2.233 ± 0.25 s, flight duration 0.40–0.65 s, and rise 0.175–0.295 m above the release center. Rise is reconstructed 0.215 m with −0.040/+0.080 m tolerance: roughly 2–3 times estimated diameter/depth error and the first airborne sample occurs after actual release. The ball must separate from every hand geom for at least 0.30 s and reach a clear apex before capture. Horizontal displacement from release center to apex must be ≤0.08 m (reconstruction <0.04 m; 0.04 m extra allows a ball-radius/contact-location difference in the larger robot hand).
  3. Spin 1, toss and catch 2. Between capture 1 and release 2 complete a directional in-hand turn of at least 2π rad. Then flight 2: release within 5.433 ± 0.25 s, capture within 5.933 ± 0.25 s, duration 0.40–0.65 s, rise 0.207–0.327 m (reference 0.247 m, same uncertainty tolerance), contact-free interval ≥0.30 s, horizontal displacement ≤0.08 m.
  4. Spin 2, toss and catch 3. Between capture 2 and release 3 complete another directional in-hand turn ≥2π rad. Then flight 3: release within 6.633 ± 0.25 s, capture within 7.200 ± 0.25 s, duration 0.45–0.72 s, rise 0.259–0.379 m (reference 0.299 m, same uncertainty tolerance), contact-free interval ≥0.30 s, horizontal displacement ≤0.08 m.
  5. Spin 3 and hold. After capture 3 complete a further directional in-hand turn ≥2π rad. Finish by 10.50 s and maintain a stable held state for the last 0.50 s (the final 15 video frames): ball-hand contact present ≥90% of samples, ball center within 0.10 m of the anatomically defined palm center, relative center speed RMS ≤0.15 m/s, relative angular speed RMS ≤1 rad/s. Thresholds define observable settling rather than a perfectly motionless numerical state. No fourth toss is allowed.

Exact event and spin measurements

A hand contact is a MuJoCo ball-to-robot contact at the integration step. A release is loss of all such contacts followed by ≥0.30 s continuously free; ignore contact chatter shorter than 0.06 s. Capture is the first subsequent ball-hand contact followed by at least 0.12 s of support (contact present ≥80%). Ballistic intervals must fit acceleration (0,0,−9.81) within 0.5 m/s² RMS, allowing numerical fitting/contact boundary error; no other forces act on the ball except physical contacts and gravity. Rise uses maximum center height minus release center height. Detect exactly three qualifying flights, in the order above.

For each spin, transform relative ball angular velocity (ball minus wrist) into the instantaneous wrist frame. Compute the principal axis of the integral of ωωᵀ over the held stage. The absolute signed integral of ω along that fixed axis must be ≥2π. This rejects back-and-forth shaking whose unsigned angular path is large. Ball-hand contact must be present ≥80% of the spin stage, and no unsupported gap may exceed 0.06 s. The 80% fraction accommodates intermittent fingertip regrasp contact seen in the demonstration; the unsupported-gap limit is under two demonstration frames. Record the axis and full angular trace. A virtual rendering seam may show simulation rotation but is not a sensing input or geometry feature.

Demonstration similarity and physical validity

Use a single fixed world alignment and anatomical retarget transform, documented in the simulation record, for every episode. The robot's +Y palm normal and −Z finger direction map to the demonstration palm normal and wrist-to-middle-MCP direction. Compare actual wrist orientation and translation with the retargeted reconstruction at the same task time, interpolating only missing reference frames; do not align each rollout independently. Require wrist rotation error RMS ≤20° and p95 ≤35°, translation error RMS ≤0.05 m and maximum ≤0.10 m. The tolerances accommodate human/robot palm geometry and monocular wrist fit error but preserve the visible palm-up behavior and roughly 0.23 m vertical dip/launch pattern. Report the palm-normal tilt distribution as well.

No ball-floor contact, ball drop, extra object, or external ball manipulation. Every finger position stays within the specified limit plus 0.02 rad compliance allowance, every speed within its exact specified maximum, every applied torque within its effort limit, and all commanded targets finite. Wrist force/torque and executed target speed limits follow hardware/SPECS.md. Check these at the 1 kHz integration/controller rate throughout the episode; post hoc clipping of logged violations cannot make an episode pass.

Evaluation scope

Nominal seed 1000 uses the documented initial state. Other seeds vary initial ball center by independent uniform ±3 mm in horizontal directions, wrist yaw by ±2°, and initial finger angle by ±0.01 rad, followed by the same 0.20 s physical settling. Encoder noise is always the specified 0.002 rad and 0.05 rad/s Gaussian. Ball geometry/mass/inertia remain the specification values. Report sensitivity to inferred friction separately; passing these ten episodes proves only this small simulation distribution, not robustness to real-world uncertainty or successful hardware transfer. A failed stage is not replaced by a later action; partial progress is reported separately from complete success.

GPU static-controller validation agrees with CPU held state within about10micrometres and benchmarks69,689policy-environment steps/s at2048worlds (20physics ticks each), versus about1000CPU steps/s per run. Full GPU baseline validation is running before a GPU simulation record and training. I also corrected final-evaluation initialization so world-frame ball jitter is independent of wrist yaw, matching criteria wording; early failed CPU evaluations rotated the nominal ball with yaw before adding jitter. No passing claim relies on those early trials.
 · r0029 · Nov 03, 02:46 EST
hypothesisMixed training now spans toss transitions and final settling. Flight rewards track physically generated baseline paths that already meet criteria, while held-stage rewards retain the anatomical…
more
Mixed training now spans toss transitions and final settling. Flight rewards track physically generated baseline paths that already meet criteria, while held-stage rewards retain the anatomical wrist/palm reference. A100-point bonus marks each supported catch in its timing window and another marks7.5rad signed spin (a training margin above2pi). A separate PPO experiment uses an AR(0.9) Gaussian action mean conditioned only on its own prior target-increment history; the conditional likelihood remains Gaussian for PPO. This tests smoother exploration without any privileged observations or execution-time planning.

Run3 completed1,001,472PPO steps in1169s on the original torsional-friction model; full and isolated-spin evaluation is now running. Run6 tests the separately recorded simulationv3 .0005m torsion hypothesis with the same wide-spin curriculum and phase-gated residuals. Run7 tests independent20-joint velocity increments because coupling MCP/PIP/DIP into finger synergies may restrict rolling. All these remain PPO-only, use deployable observations, and will be recorded on evaluation, including failures.
 · r0017 · Nov 03, 02:20 EST
hypothesisThe original .005m torsional friction length is uncalibrated and may resist tennis-ball spin too strongly. MuJoCo documents torsion as a contact-patch length…
more
The original .005m torsional friction length is uncalibrated and may resist tennis-ball spin too strongly. MuJoCo documents torsion as a contact-patch length (https://mujoco.readthedocs.io/en/3.17.0/computation/). I will test .0005m nominal, with all specified mass, geometry, inertia, sliding friction and hardware unchanged, and measure sensitivity up to .005m rather than claim either is experimentally identified. This is a physics hypothesis requiring a new simulation record, not a relaxed task criterion. Pad-focused geometric IK did not solve stable rolling, so the robust original grasp remains.

more
Geometric rolling-IK analysis (not a policy result) loses the ball within about0.3s even with pad-focused tripod grasps and center feedback; it is rejected as a teacher. Position-PPO long-spin motion is partial, and smooth synergy PPO is stable but slow. Run5 starts from run3 weights and widens the curriculum to2.18-5.38,5.94-6.60,7.20-10s, using baseline physics snapshots without extra settling. Its directional spin reward has equal per-rad/s slope in all phases (target4,18,3rad/s), addressing the much shorter second spin; no verification threshold changes.

r0004 · criteria v1Nov 03, 00:44 EST

  • 9000 characters of criteria text
Criteria text

Tennis self-verification criteria v1

These are my claims about my simulation, not an official evaluation. Written before policy training/evaluation. Sources: TASK.md, the 315-frame human clip, reconstruction v1 (to be recorded before simulation), and research/demo_measurements.json. The updated demo2sim/VERIFICATION.md was re-read on 2026-11-03 before writing this document.

Evidence and uncertainties

At 30 Hz, detached flight is frames 52–67, 163–178, and 200–216; nominal release times 1.733, 5.433, 6.667 s and catches 2.267, 5.967, 7.233 s. Boundary uncertainty is about two frames (0.067 s). Fitted apex rises above the first detached center are 0.288, 0.321, 0.300 m; durations including detached frames are 0.533, 0.533, 0.567 s. Raw independent acceleration estimates, before enforcing gravity, are 9.33, 9.97, 9.90 m/s². Flight fit center residual is 14–24 mm. Diameter 65 mm anchors metric scale; focal length is an inferred monocular prior, so systematic depth error remains.

The initial quiet hold occupies frames 0–38 (1.30 s), followed by a launch dip. After first catch, a prolonged finger regrasp/spin occurs at frames 81–153 (2.433 s inclusive). Between the second catch and third release, the available spin/regrasp time is frames 179–199 (0.700 s). After third catch, final regrasp/spin is frames 230–301 (2.400 s), followed by a quiet hold at 302–314 (0.433 s). All contact is right hand–ball, no support or second hand. Thumb and opposing fingers visibly exchange contact while the palm supports the ball.

From the fitted hand, the wrist's position spans 0.148 m forward, 0.050 m laterally, and 0.234 m vertically; peak wrist speed 1.139 m/s. Retargeting uses robot +Y = fitted palm normal, robot −Z = wrist-to-middle-MCP, and +X = Y cross Z. Initial wrist is translated to (0,0,0.65) m, with the same reconstruction world axes. The palm's tilt from upward has median 33.0°, 5–95% range 22.2–41.1°, full range 17.7–56.4°. The entire wrist orientation (including heading and distal direction), not only palm tilt, is the orientation reference. Three unsupported hand frames (46,47,113) are invalid in the reconstruction; only the derived retargeting reference interpolates these short gaps, explicitly as inference.

Ball orientation and exact human spin angle are unobservable for this nearly uniform sphere. I do not claim to have measured them. TASK.md explicitly requires three spins. I interpret a meaningful spin as at least 90° of net relative rotation during a contact-supported regrasp; this is an explicit task assumption, fixed before training. It is stricter than merely detecting nonzero angular velocity, but cannot establish exact imitation of human ball rotation.

Ordered episode tests

Physics runs at 1 kHz; metrics include every physics tick, with hardware and contact checks at that rate. Full skill duration is 10.5 s, matching the clip. A constant vertical translation aligns the reconstruction with the simulation; no per-episode best-fit time warping or rotation is allowed.

  1. Initial hold. For the first 1.20 s, the ball stays within 0.14 m of the wrist, has hand contact on at least 95% of ticks, and its center speed relative to the wrist is below 0.15 m/s on at least 90% of ticks. The video is quiet for 1.30 s; 0.10 s excludes two-frame boundary uncertainty and a small settle transient. The initial observed wrist-to-ball distance is about 0.11 m; 0.14 m permits robot versus human palm geometry. The speed bound allows approximately one ball radius of repositioning over 0.2 s, not a toss.
  2. Exactly three physical tosses and catches. A toss is a maximal interval with no ball–hand contact lasting at least 0.15 s; contact gaps shorter than 0.012 s are merged to avoid solver chatter (much shorter than a video frame). Each of the three counted flights must last 0.43–0.68 s, rise 0.24–0.38 m above its release center, have one upward-to-downward vertical-velocity crossing, and return to hand contact without floor contact. Compared with measured 0.533/0.533/0.567 s and 0.288/0.321/0.300 m, these bounds allow two-frame transition uncertainty plus 14–24 mm fitting error and robot finger geometry; they still require a substantial true ballistic toss. During each flight, least-squares vertical acceleration is −9.81 ± 0.5 m/s² and horizontal center drift from release is at most 0.08 m (video fitted horizontal motions are centimeters; allowance is roughly a ball diameter plus depth uncertainty).
  3. Timing and catches. The three releases are respectively within ±0.25 s of 1.733, 5.433, 6.667 s, and catches within ±0.25 s of 2.267, 5.967, 7.233 s. This tolerance includes measured 0.067 s boundary uncertainty and up to 0.18 s retargeted finger-closing delay; it preserves the long first regrasp and rapid second regrasp. After each catch, ball center stays within 0.14 m of wrist and hand contact is present on at least 90% of the next 0.15 s (about five video frames, enough to distinguish capture from a single bounce). A fourth qualifying toss fails.
  4. Three contact-supported spins in order. Between catch 1 and release 2, catch 2 and release 3, and catch 3 and the final 0.40 s hold, the ball must each achieve at least π/2 rad of net rotation relative to the wrist from its orientation at the start of that interval. Rotation is the SO(3) geodesic angle of R_wrist(t)^T R_ball(t) relative to its value at interval start, maximized over the interval; angular path length alone does not count. During the rotation interval, hand contact must be present on at least 90% of ticks and center remain within 0.14 m of wrist. At least two distinct hand links must contact the ball at some time in each spin, including one thumb link and one opposing finger link over the interval; they need not remain simultaneously contacting. This encodes visible finger exchanges, avoids counting a tossed rotating ball or mere whole-wrist rotation, and implements the explicit 90° assumption above.
  5. Final hold. In the last 0.40 s (video quiet hold 0.433 s), contact occupies at least 95% of ticks, center remains within 0.14 m of wrist, relative center speed is below 0.10 m/s for at least 95% of ticks, and ball angular speed relative to wrist is below 1.0 rad/s for at least 95% of ticks. Orientation is unobservable in the human final hold; the angular-speed threshold is an explicit physical interpretation of “hold,” allowing less than 23° drift in 0.40 s. No further toss is allowed.
  6. Demonstration wrist similarity. Over the whole clip, root-position RMS distance to the retargeted fitted wrist is at most 0.040 m; full wrist-orientation geodesic RMS is at most 20°, and its 95th percentile at most 30°. Palm normal must have upward component at least cos(65°) on at least 99% of ticks. The 4 cm position allowance is about half a robot palm width and covers 1–3 cm monocular/retargeting uncertainty. The orientation allowance covers the unobserved forearm roll and robot palm geometry while retaining the measured palm-up, approximately 33° tilt and heading. The 65° cap adds about 9° to the fitted maximum tilt of 56.4°, preventing an inverted or vertical hand from counting as similar.
  7. Physics and hardware. No ball–floor contact, object teleportation, non-contact object force, hidden grasp weld, or kinematic ball control. Every tick obeys hardware/SPECS.md: q within URDF limits ±0.02 rad, absolute joint speed at most each URDF speed, applied torque at most each URDF effort. Wrist force/torque and executed-target speed limits use the specified controller. Any violation fails the episode; demand saturation is reported separately. Actions must be finite. Simulation mesh/contact approximations and observation privileges are disclosed.

Evaluation protocol and verdict

Evaluate a fixed set of 20 full episodes, seeds 1000–1019, with ball initial offsets independently uniform ±2 mm, finger initial offsets ±0.01 rad, ball radius uniform 0.0315–0.0335 m (specified diameter tolerance), mass uniform ±5% around 0.0577 kg, and sliding contact coefficient uniform 0.7–0.9. Nominal physics is separately reported. These small perturbations test numerical repeatability and plausible object uncertainty; the 90% success requirement is my explicit robustness assumption. All seven episode tests must pass in order in at least 18/20 episodes, with no hardware violations in any of the 20. Report per-episode, per-criterion numbers, successful and failed rollout evidence where available, top/left/right videos, checkpoint and iteration ID, and wrist errors for every evaluated iteration. A subskill or curriculum success never counts as full-task success.

The PPO network must be closed loop and determine the reported actions. If a reference or controller is used under a residual, evaluate and disclose its performance alone; a base that meets these criteria makes that formulation inadmissible. No official score, real-robot transfer, or exact human spin reconstruction is claimed.

Criteria text

Tennis demo-to-sim self-verification criteria v1

These are my simulation criteria, not an official evaluation. Source: TASK.md and reconstruction v1 of demo/tennis_IMG_0005_h264.mp4, 30 fps. They are written before any policy evaluation.

Ordered task

  1. Start supported in a cupped right hand. Toss and catch once (video release/capture about frames53/67).
  2. Spin the ball while supported, then toss and catch again (spin frames69–163, flight164–177).
  3. Spin again while supported, then toss and catch a third time (spin178–200, flight201–216).
  4. Spin once more, and finish holding the ball (frames217–314).

A state machine accepts exactly this sequence. Spin progress before the preceding catch cannot satisfy a later stage. Additional accidental releases during spin or final hold fail that episode. Initial preparation and time spent stabilizing may vary. Maximum episode duration20 seconds is an explicit assumption allowing slower robot execution than the10.5-second human clip.

Measured completion conditions

  • Toss: no ball–hand contact for at least0.12s continuously, upward world ball-COM excursion at least0.05m above its release height, and a descending segment before capture. At apex its bottom is at least0.01m above the highest supporting palm surface directly below it. All ball motion during flight comes from gravity and collision dynamics, without constraints, attachment, state resets or object actuation. The reference has three roughly0.45–0.50s flights and about0.23m rise. The thresholds preserve clear separation by more than one ball radius and a resolved flight of120 physics ticks; lower height than human is an explicit retargeting allowance for the1m/s wrist target speed limit. Report actual heights and airtimes, rather than claiming exact amplitude matching.
  • Catch: after descending free flight, renewed ball–hand contact on at least80% of samples for0.15s; ball-COM remains within0.16m of the palm centre; mean ball speed relative to palm below0.30m/s over that interval. The ball is65mm wide and the robot fingers extend about0.1m; the distance bound includes fingertips but excludes distant floor-supported objects. The duration is roughly five demonstration frames; speed bound tolerates rolling during the regrasp.
  • Each in-hand spin: while within0.16m of palm centre and supported on at least80% of samples, integrate ball angular velocity relative to wrist over a contiguous interval of at least0.20s. The norm of the integrated rotation vector must be at least pi/2 radians, and the net change of ball orientation relative to wrist at least pi/3 radians. Angular path alone cannot satisfy the criterion through cancelling oscillations. These are explicit minimum quarter-turn/60-degree-net assumptions: the unmarked sphere's exact angle and axis are unobservable, while TASK.md explicitly requires spin. Report both values for all three spins, contact fraction and durations. Rigidly carrying a nonrotating ball with wrist rotation does not count.
  • Final hold: after the third spin, support contact on at least90% of samples for1.0s, relative speed RMS below0.15m/s, ball-COM within0.16m of palm centre. One second is a deliberate stability test beyond the brief terminal demonstration hold.
  • No loss: no floor contact, no invalid state, and no unintended contact-free interval longer than0.08s outside a declared toss/catch transition. No ball teleportation or forces other than gravity/contact.
  • Hardware: every physics step respects all20 joint positions within URDF limits plus0.02rad allowance, absolute velocities no greater than vendor limits and applied torques no greater than vendor efforts. Commands are finite and correctly shaped. Report maximum fractions of speed/effort bounds and position exceedance. Wrist actuator uses specified gains, force/torque norm bounds and executed-target speed limits.

Demonstration similarity

Retarget the reconstructed right-hand wrist using wrist-to-middle-MCP direction and the index/little-MCP palm normal to map to robot -Z/finger direction and +Y/palm normal. One constant world translation and yaw aligns the initial pose; no per-frame alignment. Compare policies at corresponding normalized sub-event phases, permitting task timing changes. Record the transformation, interpolation and time mapping with the simulation.

Require wrist position RMSE at most0.08m and orientation geodesic RMSE at most35 degrees against that reference, and outward palm normal within45 degrees of world up for at least90% of the episode. The video is predominantly palm up;8cm allows morphology/launch scaling on a roughly20cm demonstrated wrist excursion;35 degrees allows wrist-frame retargeting uncertainty while disallowing a fundamentally different grasp orientation. Report actual errors, palm-up fraction and wrist paths. Ball geometry must remain the specified65mm sphere of mass0.0577kg and inertia about4.1e-5kg m2.

Evaluation and verdict

Run12 complete episodes with held-out seeds1000–1011 after training, with ball initial horizontal displacement independently uniform±2mm, mass multiplier uniform[0.95,1.05], sliding friction uniform[0.7,1.0], encoder noise sigma0.002rad/0.05rad/s. No episode cherry-picking. These modest ranges probe local robustness because unknown felt/rubber contacts are the main modeling uncertainty. Success requires at least10/12 episodes satisfying every criterion in order. Publish per-episode and per-stage metrics and three-view videos of a success and a failure if either exists. A passing verdict is limited to this modeled distribution, not hardware or the exact human trajectory.

Ambiguities and limitations

There is no prescribed initial pose, exact timing, spin axis or angle, toss height, or final grip. Initial conditions will follow the held/palm-up reconstruction. A sphere has no observable rotational gauge in the video; orientation in simulation supplies the measurement, not a claimed reconstruction of exact spin. Object friction/restitution/compliance are inferred and disclosed. Ground-truth simulated object pose and velocity may be observed by the policy; a real visual estimator is outside this claim. No force/tactile/current observations are supplied to the policy. Criteria revisions, if any, are separate recorded versions with reasons.

Reflection

Full-sequence residual PPO meets criteria v2 in12/12 held-out episodes. The reference/base controller itself also met these criteria in a separate12/12 diagnostic; no improvement over that baseline is claimed. The final…

more
Full-sequence residual PPO meets criteria v2 in12/12 held-out episodes. The reference/base controller itself also met these criteria in a separate12/12 diagnostic; no improvement over that baseline is claimed. The final executed policy contains a nonzero, state-dependent neural residual trained by PPO, which is allowed by LEARNING.md. Main task motion comes from the reference scaffold; RL contribution is small and explicitly limited. Earlier failures drove corrections to controller coordinates, mechanical collisions, launch smoothness and spin measurement.

Limitations
  • Own simulation criteria only; no official score or hardware validation
  • 7.0–9.2cm tosses are smaller than approximately23cm reconstructed human flights
  • Wrist orientation RMS31.5deg and position RMS4.74cm meet chosen tolerances but do not imply exact motion reproduction
  • Simulated ball pose/velocities are privileged policy observations; no visual estimator
  • Contact/friction/compliance inferred; convex meshes and rigid pads approximate real hand
  • Strong reference scaffold solves this modeled distribution even without the RL residual; no RL performance gain over baseline demonstrated

Limitations
  • Tosses7.0–9.2cm vs roughly23cm human reference; this is the explicit amplitude retargeting allowance in criteria v2.
  • Wrist orientation RMS31.5deg/position4.74cm satisfy chosen tolerances; motion is not an exact replay.

r0004 · criteria v1Nov 02, 17:07 EST

  • 5123 characters of criteria text
Criteria text

Agent verification criteria v1

These are my claims about my simulation, not official success criteria. The evidence is TASK.md and reconstruction v1 of all 315 video frames. All quantities are computed from dynamic MuJoCo state and actual collision contacts, without kinematically setting the ball after reset. Every evaluation starts from the initial hold, not from a later demonstration frame.

Ordered outcomes

Complete three distinct toss–catch cycles. Between catch 1 and release 2, between catch 2 and release 3, and after catch 3, complete one in-hand spin. The final spin is followed by a stable hold. A state machine consumes these events in this order; a later event cannot replace a missing earlier event.

  • Toss: no ball–hand contact for at least 0.15 s, vertical rise from the release center at least 0.15 m, and an upward center velocity at release. The three reconstructed flight windows are 53–66, 164–178 and 200–215, lasting about 0.47–0.53 s with at least 0.21, 0.24 and 0.30 m rise from their first fitted frame. A 0.15 m rise and 0.15 s separation are explicit robot allowances, chosen below the smallest observed flight but well beyond contact bounce. Each flight must end in a catch; floor contact fails the episode.
  • Catch: actual hand contact, ball center within 0.16 m of the mount frame, and ball speed relative to the wrist below 0.30 m/s for at least 0.12 s, allowing contact on 70% of samples in that interval. The distance includes the roughly 0.1 m palm/finger reach plus the 32.5 mm radius; the speed and dwell are explicit assumptions to distinguish arrested flight from a glancing collision.
  • In-hand spin: before the next release, or before final hold, the ball's orientation relative to the wrist changes by at least pi/2 radians from its orientation at the start of that spin stage. The ball remains within 0.16 m of the wrist with hand contact in at least 70% of the stage's samples. This is a net relative rotation, not accumulated oscillation and not rotation of the wrist carrying a fixed ball. TASK.md requires spins but states no angle or axis; 90 degrees is my explicit conservative assumption. No recovered spin angle is claimed from the video.
  • Final hold: after the third spin, maintain the ball within 0.16 m of the wrist, relative speed below 0.10 m/s and hand contact on at least 70% of samples for 0.50 s. The longer dwell extends the short final video hold to test stability. The ball must remain above the floor.

Demonstration similarity and hardware

Retarget the human wrist with its origin at joint 0, forward finger direction from wrist to middle MCP, and palm normal from (index MCP−wrist) cross (little MCP−wrist). Map this frame to the right robot's −Z finger direction and +Y palm normal. Translate the initial human wrist to the chosen robot starting position; keep metric displacements and time. The policy may use an explicitly recorded uniform time scale; compare at that same phase. Evaluate the entire episode, including any early termination (which is a task failure).

  • Wrist position RMS error at most 0.07 m and orientation geodesic RMS error at most 25 degrees relative to the retargeted reference. These are explicit allowances for monocular depth error, human-to-robot geometry, and dynamic control; reconstructed wrist vertical range is 0.232 m, so 7 cm still requires following the toss motion.
  • Palm normal dot world up at least 0.5 for at least 95% of the episode. The reconstructed normal is 0.60–0.96 with median 0.86. A 60-degree tilt allowance retains a cupped upward-facing hand.
  • No finger hardware violation: every recorded 1 kHz physics step respects position lower−0.02 to upper+0.02, absolute speed at most the URDF limit, and applied torque at most the effort limit, per hardware/SPECS.md. Targets are finite and clipped to joint limits. Wrist force/torque and target-rate saturation are recorded and follow the specified controller.

Success means every ordered outcome, similarity threshold and hardware condition is met in a single episode. Report counts for tosses, catches, spins and final hold, plus numerical similarity and hardware results. Partial progress is diagnostic and never a success.

Evaluation distribution and limits

Use 20 fixed evaluation seeds (1000–1019), with initial ball position offsets uniformly within ±2 mm horizontally, ±1 mm vertically, friction coefficient multiplier uniform [0.9,1.1], and mass multiplier [0.95,1.05]; report nominal rollouts separately if used. Initial ball orientation is uniformly random (unmarked sphere). Encoder noise is the hardware Gaussian noise. No contacts, forces, current or tactile measurements enter the actor. If exact object pose and velocity enter the actor, identify this as privileged simulation sensing. Report a Wilson 95% interval on full success rate.

This cannot establish real-world transfer, real contact compliance, robustness to large placement errors, or a recovered human spin angle. Camera focal length remains prior-driven. Any simulator or criterion changes receive a new record before dependent evaluation.

Reflection

Phase-local PPO and the feedback launch/catch base controller produced partial sequences: at most two ordered tosses, one catch and one spin; 0/20 full successes. All 20 seeds satisfy finger hardware limits, but only…

more
Phase-local PPO and the feedback launch/catch base controller produced partial sequences: at most two ordered tosses, one catch and one spin; 0/20 full successes. All 20 seeds satisfy finger hardware limits, but only 10/20 satisfy wrist similarity. Mean stage progress is lower than the zero-residual analysis base controller, while episode survival and speed margin improve. This reveals a retention bias rather than successful task learning. Iteration 4 adds explicit ordered-stage rewards with unchanged thresholds and identical physics.

Smoother residual exploration and improved PPO scaling produced full-duration retention and hardware compliance in all fixed evaluation episodes, but the policy retained the ball instead of tossing. No qualifying ordered tosses and 0/20 complete successes. The next experiment uses separately recorded sim v3: a physically feasible launch/catch base controller, finer finger-command interpolation and local phase curricula; the final policy remains an RL-trained closed-loop network residual.

Limitations
  • Agent-defined criteria v1, not official evaluation.
  • Privileged exact ball-state sensing; no real-world transfer shown.
  • The same 20 fixed seeds are reused for comparison and selection, not an independent held-out test.
  • Convex collision hulls and inferred rigid-pad contact properties.
  • Reference camera focal is prior-driven; human spin angle not observable.
  • No successful episode is claimed when none satisfies every ordered outcome.

Criteria text

Verification criteria v2

These are my own simulation criteria for TASK.md, not an official evaluation. They are recorded before evaluating a policy. All criteria must pass in each of ten complete episodes, seeds 1000–1009, with initial object XY independently perturbed uniformly by ±3 mm and yaw by ±2 degrees, object masses independently ±5%, plastic friction ±10%, and the specified encoder noise. The fixed evaluation seeds will not be used for PPO rollouts. Nominal results and a reference-controller ablation will also be reported.

Evidence: video 436 frames at 30 fps (14.53 s), manual event inspection, reconstruction v2, object/SPECS.md and TASK.md. Approximate video contact intervals are white frames 70–214 (2.33–7.13 s), black 260–385 (8.67–12.83 s), with ±5-frame transition uncertainty. White begins turning at about 3.33 s and is blades-up by 4.57 s; black turns at about 9.90–11.10 s. The final unsupported black rest lasts about 1.67 s; white rests unsupported for over 7 s. The reconstructed horizontal transfers are white 0.276 m and black 0.284 m, mostly along +Y. Estimated visible pose uncertainty is 25 mm and 12 degrees; hidden turns are not observations. Peak reconstructed surface clearances are approximately 24 mm (white) and 61 mm (black), but depth is uncertain. Thresholds below use instruction-exact side and direction conditions plus physically meaningful tolerances.

  1. Initial state and order. Both plugs start on the right (body_y <= 0.15 m) on a broad side, blade axes within 15 degrees of horizontal, without hand contact. The white plug must be grasped, lifted, transferred, placed, and released before the black plug is lifted. The video performs these actions sequentially with about 1.5 s between white release and black lift. A black lift before white release fails.
  1. A physical pickup for each plug. The lowest point of every body/blade collision box must exceed tabletop height by at least 5 mm continuously for at least 0.25 s; peak clearance must reach at least 10 mm white and 35 mm black. White measured peak is about 24 mm; black about 61 mm, with centimetric monocular uncertainty. The 5 mm continuous margin exceeds contact compliance and prevents a slide being counted as pickup. The 0.25 s interval is shorter than the clearly observed airborne manipulation (at least 0.5 s each), allowing contact-transition uncertainty. During an airborne interval, the plug must have contact with the thumb and at least one opposing long finger for at least 80% of samples. A contact sample requires physical robot–object contact from the simulator, never an attachment constraint. The opposing-contact rule comes from the visible thumb/finger pinch, especially black at 9.3–12.5 s.
  1. Transfer left and turn blades up. Each plug's body center must move at least 0.20 m in +Y from its initial pose and finish strictly at y > 0.15 m. Reconstructed transfers are about 0.27–0.28 m; 0.20 m allows twice the 25 mm position uncertainty and imperfect morphology retargeting, while preserving the approximately 25 cm transfer in demo/README.md. The blade axis must be within 10 degrees of world +Z at placement. The demonstrated final orientations are visually upright; 10 degrees is tighter than reconstruction orientation uncertainty and leaves a positive static stability margin for these narrow bases.
  1. Place and release both. In the last continuous 1.5 s, both plugs must have body-bottom height within 2 mm of the table, blade tilt <=10 degrees, linear speed <0.02 m/s and angular speed <0.10 rad/s. Neither plug may contact the hand during this interval, and minimum hand–object separation must exceed 5 mm. Both must remain at y >0.15 m; horizontal drift over this interval must be <3 mm. The video shows black unsupported and stationary for about 1.67 s. The 2 mm support tolerance covers the rigid contact solver; 3 mm drift is approximately one percent of transfer distance, comparable to the image's stationary-object pixel uncertainty. Speed limits make settling measurable rather than judging one lucky frame. White must remain upright during the black manipulation, allowing tilt <=15 degrees transiently and no return to the right side.
  1. Wrist and skill similarity. A single fixed rotation from the MANO root frame to an anatomy-based palm frame maps the human palm normal to robot +Y and wrist-to-middle-MCP direction to robot −Z. It is fitted once across valid hand frames, then held constant; positions use the simulator tabletop transform and the fixed robot mount-to-palm offset. Reference wrists are interpolated only across invalid gaps, labelled inferred. Compare actual wrist poses with this retargeted reference at the same normalized phase (approach, grasp/lift/turn, carry, place/release), allowing a maximum ±0.25 s phase boundary shift, the video transition uncertainty plus 0.08 s for control response. Across valid reference frames during manipulation, wrist orientation geodesic RMS must be <=20 degrees and its 90th percentile <=30 degrees; position RMS <=40 mm. The selected hand fit differs from the HaWoR initialization by about 14.5 degrees in median palm orientation. Object orientation uncertainty is about 12 degrees, and the fixed anatomy mapping accounts for human–robot palm axes; 20 degrees allows this estimated pose error while preserving the palm-down/tilted-wrist skill. The 40 mm position tolerance covers 25 mm depth uncertainty plus the morphology offset's remaining fit error. Report palm-normal tilt and wrist roll separately for both plugs. A palm-up scoop, table push, throw, or arm-like teleport does not qualify merely by achieving the endpoint.
  1. Dynamics and hardware. All object motion must arise from gravity, table contact and robot contact. No weld, magnet, grasp attachment, object pose setter, hidden force, or runtime planner may drive the plugs. The floating wrist uses wrist-1 at 1 kHz, 30 N/2 N·m limits and target rate limits; fingers use the specified PD gains, effort saturation and URDF position/speed limits. Check every 1 ms physics tick against finger position allowances, maximum speeds and applied torque limits. Any hardware violation fails that episode. The verified actor observes only permitted proprioception, previous targets, wrist state, object states, step index and constants, and its trainable network has been updated with PPO. Baseline performance, PPO learning curves, checkpoint and observation/action definitions must be recorded.

Complete each episode within 16 s. This retains the demonstration's 14.53 s action sequence with less than 1.5 s extra settling; the extra time does not change subgoal order. Per-criterion measurements, event timestamps, joint extrema, wrist errors and object paths must be saved for all ten episodes. Save top/left/right videos of success and any failure. Passing ten episodes is evidence only for this simulator and this narrow perturbation range; it does not establish real-hand transfer or robustness to unmeasured physics.

Ambiguities: video does not identify friction, inertia, exact hidden contacts or precise depth. Those parameters are labelled assumptions and randomized as above; object dimensions, masses and COM preserve public specifications. The robot has a free wrist and no arm; a constant wrist-frame mapping and bounded tracking error are used to assess similarity. No precise target XY location is prescribed beyond the left-side condition and demonstrated transfer distance. There is no insertion into a socket.

Revision reason: reconstruction v2 adds the missing all-vertex hand–table check and corrects wrist/hand penetration. It replaces v1 as the wrist reference. All numerical pass thresholds, evaluation seeds, perturbations and task requirements remain identical. No policy has yet been evaluated or trained.

The opposing-contact rule comes from the visible thumb/finger pinch, especially black at 9.3–12.5 s.
  1. Transfer left and turn blades up. Each plug's body center must move at least 0.20 m in +Y from its initial pose and finish strictly at y > 0.15 m. Reconstructed transfers are about 0.27–0.28 m; 0.20 m allows twice the 25 mm position uncertainty and imperfect morphology retargeting, while preserving the approximately 25 cm transfer in demo/README.md. The blade axis must be within 10 degrees of world +Z at placement. The demonstrated final orientations are visually upright; 10 degrees is tighter than reconstruction orientation uncertainty and leaves a positive static stability margin for these narrow bases.
  1. Place and release both. In the last continuous 1.5 s, both plugs must have body-bottom height within 2 mm of the table, blade tilt <=10 degrees, linear speed <0.02 m/s and angular speed <0.10 rad/s. Neither plug may contact the hand during this interval, and minimum hand–object separation must exceed 5 mm. Both must remain at y >0.15 m; horizontal drift over this interval must be <3 mm. The video shows black unsupported and stationary for about 1.67 s. The 2 mm support tolerance covers the rigid contact solver; 3 mm drift is approximately one percent of transfer distance, comparable to the image's stationary-object pixel uncertainty. Speed limits make settling measurable rather than judging one lucky frame. White must remain upright during the black manipulation, allowing tilt <=15 degrees transiently and no return to the right side.
  1. Wrist and skill similarity. A single fixed rotation from the MANO root frame to an anatomy-based palm frame maps the human palm normal to robot +Y and wrist-to-middle-MCP direction to robot −Z. It is fitted once across valid hand frames, then held constant; positions use the simulator tabletop transform and the fixed robot mount-to-palm offset. Reference wrists are interpolated only across invalid gaps, labelled inferred. Compare actual wrist poses with this retargeted reference at the same normalized phase (approach, grasp/lift/turn, carry, place/release), allowing a maximum ±0.25 s phase boundary shift, the video transition uncertainty plus 0.08 s for control response. Across valid reference frames during manipulation, wrist orientation geodesic RMS must be <=20 degrees and its 90th percentile <=30 degrees; position RMS <=40 mm. The selected hand fit differs from the HaWoR initialization by about 12.1 degrees in median palm orientation. Object orientation uncertainty is about 12 degrees, and the fixed anatomy mapping accounts for human–robot palm axes; 20 degrees allows this estimated pose error while preserving the palm-down/tilted-wrist skill. The 40 mm position tolerance covers 25 mm depth uncertainty plus the morphology offset's remaining fit error. Report palm-normal tilt and wrist roll separately for both plugs. A palm-up scoop, table push, throw, or arm-like teleport does not qualify merely by achieving the endpoint.
  1. Dynamics and hardware. All object motion must arise from gravity, table contact and robot contact. No weld, magnet, grasp attachment, object pose setter, hidden force, or runtime planner may drive the plugs. The floating wrist uses wrist-1 at 1 kHz, 30 N/2 N·m limits and target rate limits; fingers use the specified PD gains, effort saturation and URDF position/speed limits. Check every 1 ms physics tick against finger position allowances, maximum speeds and applied torque limits. Any hardware violation fails that episode. The verified actor observes only permitted proprioception, previous targets, wrist state, object states, step index and constants, and its trainable network has been updated with PPO. Baseline performance, PPO learning curves, checkpoint and observation/action definitions must be recorded.

Complete each episode within 16 s. This retains the demonstration's 14.53 s action sequence with less than 1.5 s extra settling; the extra time does not change subgoal order. Per-criterion measurements, event timestamps, joint extrema, wrist errors and object paths must be saved for all ten episodes. Save top/left/right videos of success and any failure. Passing ten episodes is evidence only for this simulator and this narrow perturbation range; it does not establish real-hand transfer or robustness to unmeasured physics.

Ambiguities: video does not identify friction, inertia, exact hidden contacts or precise depth. Those parameters are labelled assumptions and randomized as above; object dimensions, masses and COM preserve public specifications. The robot has a free wrist and no arm; a constant wrist-frame mapping and bounded tracking error are used to assess similarity. No precise target XY location is prescribed beyond the left-side condition and demonstrated transfer distance. There is no insertion into a socket.

Criteria text

Agent-defined verification criteria, version 2

These are my own simulation claims, derived from TASK.md, the demonstration, and reconstruction version 1. This version clarifies continuous hand support and numerical contact handling before any RL policy is trained or evaluated. They are not official evaluation criteria. They are recorded before any policy is evaluated.

Evidence and ordered task plan

The video shows a right-hand approach, white-body grasp and lift (approximately frames 73–115), white reorientation/leftward carry (116–175), white set-down/release (176–220), return to black (221–260), black grasp/lift/reorientation (261–315), black carry/lower (316–367), release (368–393), and two upright chargers after withdrawal (394–435). Exact contact timing and hidden finger articulation are estimated. TASK.md explicitly requires white first, then black, transferred from right to left, blades upward, and demonstration-like wrist poses. The scene defines left as body-center y>0.15 m.

All distances below are metres and all time requirements are continuous simulation time. Objects have exactly the specified dimensions and state-frame origin. A body bottom is the minimum world z of its eight body-box corners. Blade-up angle is acos(dot(R_object[:,2], world_up)). Thresholds below are explicit physical/tolerance assumptions, not measured ground truth.

  1. Initial state and physical grasp. Both chargers start on their sides on the table's right, from the reconstruction's initial positions and orientations mapped into the simulation. White is manipulated first. Before each lift, the thumb and at least one of index/middle/ring/little establish simultaneous contacts with that charger for >=0.10 s, each with normal force >=0.05 N. Contact position vectors from its body center subtend >=60 degrees. This distinguishes an opposing grasp from a one-sided push; 0.05 N is a small but resolvable contact relative to 0.54–0.74 N object weights, and 0.10 s excludes a single collision impulse.
  2. White lift and transfer. After its grasp, white's body bottom clears the tabletop by >=0.015 m for >=0.15 s, without table contact. Its center moves in +Y by >=0.20 m. The 15 mm clearance is a visible, physically meaningful lift rather than sliding; the demonstration's lateral transfer is about 0.25 m, with 0.20 m allowing monocular scale uncertainty. Held carry clarification (both chargers). From the lift event until first table set-down, whenever body-bottom clearance exceeds 5 mm, a hand contact patch with normal force >=0.05 N must support the charger; no unsupported interval may exceed 0.05 s. This rules out tossing and prolonged slipping while allowing short contact transitions during finger repositioning. The demonstration shows hand support throughout transport.
  3. White placement and release, before black. White reaches y>0.15, blade-up angle <=15 degrees, and body bottom in [-0.002,+0.002]. It has table normal support >=0.10 N, zero hand contacts, and speed <=0.01 m/s and angular speed <=0.15 rad/s for >=0.50 s before the black grasp begins. Its body center remains on the left and blade-up angle <=20 degrees throughout the black manipulation. Fifteen degrees is well inside the tipping angle of these bases; the extra 5 degrees during the second transfer tolerates brief settling. The 2 mm support band covers contact compliance while excluding floating/sinking.
  4. Black lift and transfer. Black's opposing grasp follows completed white placement, then the same >=15 mm, >=0.15 s lift and >=0.20 m +Y transport apply. Black must not achieve the lift event before white release. This enforces the demonstrated ordering.
  5. Black placement and final independent standing. Black reaches y>0.15 and the same placement bounds. Both chargers then meet the following together for >=2.0 s: blade-up angle <=15 degrees, body bottom in [-0.002,+0.002], table support >=0.10 N each, linear speed <=0.01 m/s, angular speed <=0.15 rad/s, position drift <=0.005 m over the hold, zero hand contacts, and minimum geometric hand–object separation >=0.010 m. Neither contacts the floor. Independent table support and hand separation ensure the hand is not secretly holding them. The 2 s hold is longer than the video's final visible stand and tests stability.
  6. Demonstration-like wrist. Retarget the fitted human wrist using axes: robot -Z follows wrist-to-MCP-centroid, robot +Y is the right palm normal (cross of wrist-to-index-MCP and wrist-to-little-MCP), robot +X completes the right-handed frame; position is the fitted wrist. Apply the same fixed reconstruction-to-table rigid alignment as the objects. For each charger separately, align the interval from grasp onset to placement/release linearly to the reconstructed contact interval (white 73–217, black 261–388), without dynamic time warping. On frames with valid reconstructed hand poses, require full wrist-orientation geodesic RMS <=40 degrees, 95th percentile <=65 degrees, and wrist-position RMS <=0.08 m. Report palm-normal error as well. These tolerances acknowledge 12–35 degree monocular object/hand ambiguity, robot/human anatomical differences, and the floating mount offset; they still require the same broad palm-down/oblique wrist behavior. The initial 0.20 s of white grasp additionally requires mean palm normal dot world-down >=0.50; black >=0.20, matching its more oblique approach.
  7. Hardware and physical integrity. No joint position, speed, applied torque, finite-action or controller-limit violations under hardware/SPECS.md. Saturated demands are reported. Objects are passive free rigid bodies throughout execution: no pose assignment after reset, welds, grasp constraints, or applied object forces. All movement must follow contact and gravity. These are invariants of the claim, not task rewards.

Contact quantities are sampled at the 1 kHz physics rate. Numerical zero contact means no contact patch normal force exceeds 1e-5 N. Event times are resolved to 1 ms. Wrist-similarity alignment ends at the start of the uninterrupted 0.50 s released-placement interval, and the placement is completed at its end.

Episode, cohort, and pass rule

Each episode has at most 40 s, about 2.75 times the human clip, allowing the specified actuator limits and a 2 s stability hold. Success means every criterion above holds, in order, before timeout. No partial completion is a pass.

Verification uses 20 fresh episodes: episode 0 is nominal; episodes 1–19 independently sample initial object X/Y offsets Uniform[-0.002,+0.002] m, world-yaw offsets Uniform[-2,+2] degrees, mass multipliers Uniform[0.95,1.05], and sliding friction Uniform[0.70,0.90]. The 1 kHz controllers and specified 500 Hz Gaussian encoder noise remain active. Fixed evaluation seeds are 10000–10019; evaluation uses the network's mean action. These small ranges test local repeatability, not broad real-world robustness. The overall verdict passes only if nominal succeeds, >=16/20 episodes meet all task/wrist criteria, and all 20 episodes meet hardware/integrity invariants. Save per-episode and per-criterion metrics and top/left/right videos of success and failure where present.

Ambiguities and limitations

Final X/Y spacing, exact timing, permitted robot finger strategy, friction, inertia, and tolerances are not prescribed. We choose nearby nonoverlapping placements reconstructed from the final video and allow slower execution. Wrist similarity is quantitative but toleranced; it does not prove identical hidden in-hand rolling. Simulation contacts, estimated masses, and absent sensing/actuator details limit any real-robot inference. The final controller must include a closed-loop network trained with reinforcement learning; residual RL on a reconstruction-derived base is allowed by LEARNING.md and will be stated explicitly.

more
Iteration2 (1.505M PPO transitions on the full white sequence) still has0/20 full successes. All20 acquire an opposing white grasp and lift, but none maintain held carry or complete placement; the best nominal blade-up error is about62.8deg before slipping. No black grasp succeeds, and the untrained later phase produces middle-PIP speed violations. Planned-clock wrist diagnostics improve to mean position RMS0.0769m white/0.0774m black and white orientation RMS39.2deg; without completed release these are diagnostics, not a passing wrist criterion. The changed offline finger path and partial wrist turn can still abandon a real grasp. Next: anchor the finger reference to the physically achieved grasp, train reorientation from a validated passive held-grasp reset, and give the network independent residual control of all20 finger joints. Keep the original20-episode task/wrist/hardware criteria. Force-allocation analysis produced partial in-hand rotation but its weaker-posture variant dropped the object; it is not a solution or a reported policy.

Limitations
  • All claims refer to this constructed simulation, not official evaluation or real hardware.
  • Perfect simulated object pose observations; uncertain friction/inertia/contact compliance.

PPO iteration 1 learned the white opposing grasp, >=15 mm lift and >=20 cm left transfer in all20 evaluation episodes, where the zero-residual baseline failed the lift. Full success is0/20: white is released sideways, and corrections learned only on the white lift interfere with black placement. All20 hardware/integrity checks pass. Mean wrist orientation RMS is about10.6deg white/15.7deg black; position RMS0.0857m/0.0814m exceeds the recorded0.08m bound. Do not relax criteria. Next: train the entire white manipulation with phase-gated lift/contact rewards, stronger blade-axis and released-standing rewards, and a direct human-wrist-position reward. The frozen white base still underdrives rotation; revise its offline retargeting to share a modest, explicitly measured extra wrist rotation with finger rolling, while retaining the same wrist thresholds. Then train the whole two-object sequence and expand randomization.

Iteration2 (1.505M PPO transitions on the full white sequence) still has0/20 full successes. All20 acquire an opposing white grasp and lift, but none maintain held carry or complete placement; the best nominal blade-up error is about62.8deg before slipping. No black grasp succeeds, and the untrained later phase produces middle-PIP speed violations. Planned-clock wrist diagnostics improve to mean position RMS0.0769m white/0.0774m black and white orientation RMS39.2deg; without completed release these are diagnostics, not a passing wrist criterion. The changed offline finger path and partial wrist turn can still abandon a real grasp. Next: anchor the finger reference to the physically achieved grasp, train reorientation from a validated passive held-grasp reset, and give the network independent residual control of all20 finger joints. Keep the original20-episode task/wrist/hardware criteria. Force-allocation analysis produced partial in-hand rotation but its weaker-posture variant dropped the object; it is not a solution or a reported policy.

Limitations
  • All claims refer to this constructed simulation, not official evaluation or real hardware.
  • Perfect simulated object pose observations; uncertain friction/inertia/contact compliance.

PPO iteration 1 learned the white opposing grasp, >=15 mm lift and >=20 cm left transfer in all20 evaluation episodes, where the zero-residual baseline failed the lift. Full success is0/20: white is released sideways,…

more
PPO iteration 1 learned the white opposing grasp, >=15 mm lift and >=20 cm left transfer in all20 evaluation episodes, where the zero-residual baseline failed the lift. Full success is0/20: white is released sideways, and corrections learned only on the white lift interfere with black placement. All20 hardware/integrity checks pass. Mean wrist orientation RMS is about10.6deg white/15.7deg black; position RMS0.0857m/0.0814m exceeds the recorded0.08m bound. Do not relax criteria. Next: train the entire white manipulation with phase-gated lift/contact rewards, stronger blade-axis and released-standing rewards, and a direct human-wrist-position reward. The frozen white base still underdrives rotation; revise its offline retargeting to share a modest, explicitly measured extra wrist rotation with finger rolling, while retaining the same wrist thresholds. Then train the whole two-object sequence and expand randomization.

Limitations
  • All claims refer to this constructed simulation, not official evaluation or real hardware.
  • Perfect simulated object pose observations; uncertain friction/inertia/contact compliance.

The original approach/lift RL actor already succeeds locally; isolated rotation training can damage actions on phases it never visits. Proposed architecture: a phase-gated mixture of closed-loop PPO-trained neural actors for acquisition, white reorientation/placement, and black manipulation. Each command residual still comes from an RL-trained network, while the same reconstruction-derived reference and exact hardware PD execute it. This is a hierarchical residual-RL architecture, not a scripted final policy or online optimizer. A full original-state20episode evaluation will judge the composed policy; curriculum progress alone cannot pass.

Planned learning approach (not yet building the training simulation): a reconstruction-derived wrist/finger reference plus a closed-loop neural residual trained by PPO. This is explicitly permitted by LEARNING.md; scripted replay is a baseline only. The policy will observe noisy encoders, wrist state, object pose estimates and phase, and supply action corrections through the specified impedance/PD controllers. Objects remain passive contact-driven rigid bodies. I will compare a zero-residual ablation and keep task, wrist and hardware metrics separate. Primary methods: https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.06347 (PPO), https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.03201 (residual RL), https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.08050 (residual RL from demonstrations). MuJoCo model semantics: https://mujoco.readthedocs.io/en/latest/XMLreference.html .

Testing a documented local copy of the required MANO fitter with explicit opposed thumb/finger surface contact and distal-finger separation penalties. The installed tools remain unchanged; these checks are not waived.

Criteria text

Agent verification criteria v1 — D2S-PLUG-1

These are my own simulation criteria, not an official evaluation. They derive from TASK.md, the video, and reconstruction v1. They are specified before evaluating an RL policy. All quantities use the task world (+Y left, table z=0), body-centred object frames, and physical simulated contacts.

Evidence and ordered task plan

The video shows white handling approximately frames 78–215 (2.6–7.17 s), then black handling approximately 279–385 (9.3–12.83 s). Initially both lie on a side. At the end both stand on their USB ends with blades upward. The hand initially approaches palm down, turns during each grasp, translates left and withdraws after placement. Exact hidden rotations and some contact details remain reconstruction estimates.

  1. Approach and grasp white. Lift it clear of the desk while supported by the hand.
  2. Reorient white with blades upward, carry it to the left side, lower, release and let it stand.
  3. Reach back to black, grasp and lift it after white has been released and stood stably.
  4. Reorient black with blades upward, carry it beside white on the left, lower and release.
  5. Withdraw and leave both standing stably, without disturbing white during black handling.

This plan specifies outcomes and order, not a robot trajectory. Contact and release boundaries have approximately five-frame visual uncertainty.

Exact quantities and thresholds

  • Initial state: both body centres have y ≤ 0.15 m. Both blade axes are within 20° of horizontal. Initial poses come from the reconstructed rest poses mapped rigidly to the task table. These checks establish the requested right-to-left task rather than starting with completed objects. The 20° allowance permits estimated table tilt and slight resting tilt; the nominal reconstruction is nearly horizontal.
  • Acquisition and pickup, separately for each plug: at least one thumb contact and at least one contact from another finger occur simultaneously for at least 0.05 s. The plug's lowest collision-shape point subsequently reaches z ≥ 0.020 m for at least 0.10 s while some hand contact persists. The 2 cm clearance exceeds the 16–18 mm blade length and contact tolerances, distinguishing a pickup from sliding. The brief dwell rejects one-tick contact and bounce artifacts. The two-sided contact requirement follows the visually opposed grasp; it is an explicit physical verification assumption where reconstructed contact is uncertain.
  • Upright left placement, separately for each plug: body-centre y > 0.15 m, angle acos(local +Z · world +Z) ≤ 15°, lowest body-box point within ±0.002 m of the desk, table contact present, and no hand contact. These conditions hold continuously for at least 0.50 s, with body-centre speed ≤ 0.010 m/s and angular speed ≤ 0.20 rad/s throughout. Left and blades-up follow TASK.md exactly. The angle is a stability margin below the approximately 24–28° static tipping angle for these bases; 2 mm covers compliant contact settling without accepting floating. The velocities allow small solver/contact settling. Half a second is an explicit stability assumption, longer than a transient frame.
  • Order and preservation: white pickup precedes its placement; white completes the above release-and-stability interval before black pickup begins; black then completes pickup and placement. Both placement conditions hold throughout the final 0.50 s. White's centre stays on the left after its placement. This follows “Do the same with the black plug” and the observed sequence. Progress is the number of completed ordered stages out of four (white pickup, white placement, black pickup, black placement).
  • Wrist resemblance: compare the actual floating wrist to the recorded retargeted human wrist, at corresponding episode phase, on supported human-hand frames. The retargeted orientation maps the wrist-to-middle-MCP axis to robot −Z and the thumb side to robot +X, with robot +Y pointing out of the palm. Report translation RMSE and mean/p95/max SO(3) angle. Require translation RMSE ≤ 0.050 m, mean rotation error ≤ 30°, and p95 rotation error ≤ 60°. Report the full curves, not only these averages. The position tolerance accommodates the 8–20 mm object depth assumptions and human/robot palm dimensions; the angular tolerances are explicit retargeting assumptions allowing anatomical differences while retaining palm-down approaches and the demonstrated turning direction. No independent wrist workspace constraint is imposed.
  • Finger hardware and valid control: zero samples outside URDF position bounds plus the 0.02 rad allowance, zero samples above URDF speed limits or effort limits, and all target vectors finite with 20 entries. Evaluate at every 1 ms physics/controller tick; wrist commands obey the prescribed speed and wrench clipping. A hardware violation makes the episode unsuccessful regardless of object progress. Thresholds come directly from hardware/SPECS.md and hardware/RIGHT_HAND.md.

Success means every criterion holds in the stated order in the same full episode. Report pickup, placement, ordering, wrist and hardware results separately so a partial behavior cannot be described as task success. No geometric attachment, pose overwrite or direct external force may move a plug during evaluation.

Evaluation and assumptions

Use 16 fixed evaluation seeds (1000–1015), full episodes, with policy sampling disabled. Seed 1000 is nominal. Other episodes perturb both initial object XY coordinates independently uniformly within ±5 mm and yaw within ±5°. Nominal masses and geometry remain specified; report any separate robustness evaluation separately. These small disturbances test closed-loop correction rather than broad sim-to-real robustness. Report mean success, counts, per-episode metrics, hardware violations and representative successful and failed rollouts from top, left and right views.

The instruction leaves exact locations, azimuth, finger choice, travel time and final spacing open. I require the specified side, upright orientation, physical pickup and stable release, without a precise goal point or yaw. Episode duration and reference time scaling will be recorded with the simulator before training. The actor may use ideal object pose estimates; any result therefore depends on this observation assumption. Uncertain monocular depth, contact modelling and the reference hand's remaining fitting limitations prevent a physical-robot claim.

Criteria text

Agent-defined simulation criteria v2

These are my claims about my simulation, not an official evaluation. Evidence: TASK.md's four clockwise 180-degree turns and finger-pair sequence, source frames 0–179, and reconstruction v1. The source's final long hold is truncated; the hold duration below is an explicit task-completion assumption.

The initial state must be a pen held between index and middle, chosen from the start of the retargeted reconstruction. No external fixtures, pen constraints, object-pose forces, or floor support may assist the policy. The complete trial lasts 10 seconds: the six-second reference is slowed by 1.5 and followed by a one-second final hold. Time scaling is allowed because timing is not prescribed.

Measurements

Let u be the pen's directed local +X axis. Project u into the fixed frame-0 demonstration camera plane, mapped into the simulation world by the recorded rigid retargeting. Angle increases clockwise in that camera's display grid. Unwrap angle at 500 Hz and subtract the initial heading to obtain theta. Projection norm must exceed 0.25 throughout each accepted rotation; otherwise that interval cannot establish heading. This excludes near-axis singularities. Axial roll does not count as pen spinning.

A finger supports the pen when an actual collision contact between that finger's links and the pen carries at least 0.02 N normal force. Two fingers establish a pair after both support it for 0.04 s continuously. During establishment, total normal force from the other two long fingers must be less than half the weaker active finger's force, and thumb normal force must be below 0.02 N. This explicit dominance assumption excludes counting a constant multi-finger cage as all four instructed pair transfers. The force threshold is about one tenth of the pen's 0.216 N weight, excluding solver chatter; 0.04 s spans 20 policy samples. These are explicit physical assumptions.

Ordered requirements

  1. Initial support: index–middle pair established within the first 0.3 s.
  2. Turn 1: theta reaches pi ±25 degrees and middle–ring support is established while heading is in that interval.
  3. Turn 2: theta reaches 2 pi ±25 degrees and ring–pinky support is established while heading is in that interval.
  4. Turn 3: theta reaches 3 pi ±25 degrees and middle–ring support is established while heading is in that interval.
  5. Turn 4: theta reaches 4 pi ±25 degrees and index–middle support is established while heading is in that interval.
  6. Hold: for the final 0.5 s, heading stays within 25 degrees of 4 pi, pen angular speed is below 1 rad/s in at least 95% of samples, pen-centre excursion is below 10 mm, and index–middle support is present in at least 80% of samples.

The heading tolerance accommodates the reconstruction's endpoint uncertainty and observed holds' small reversals without accepting a missed half-turn. Stages are accepted once, in this order. Completing later rotation milestones before the required pair has been established does not skip a stage.

Requirements across the complete trial

  • Control and retention: no pen–floor contact, pen bottom above 10 mm, and pen centre stays within 180 mm of the palm-frame origin. That radius includes the half-length 97.5 mm plus a long-finger reach; 10 mm is a floor-clearance assumption. No artificial pen attachment or prescribed pen motion.
  • Predominantly clockwise: accumulated backward heading increments, after ignoring increments below 0.5 degrees, total at most 180 degrees. The video includes repositioning and a reversal around frames 128–140; this generous assumption still requires the ordered 720-degree net result.
  • Wrist similarity: against the recorded wrist reference at k=min(179, floor(30 t/1.5)), wrist translation RMS <=40 mm and orientation RMS <=25 degrees, with maximum orientation error <=45 degrees. These tolerate uncertain monocular depth and morphology while penalizing wrist-driven spins. Report all three continuous errors even on failed trials.
  • Hardware: every finger sample respects the hardware/SPECS.md position limits with 0.02 rad allowance, speed limits without allowance, and applied effort limits. Actions are finite, correctly shaped, and returned on time. Saturated demand is reported separately. A violation fails the trial.

Success requires every ordered and trial-wide requirement. Progress is the number of accepted ordered support/turn stages (0–5), plus separately reported net turns and retention time. Reward and return alone never establish success.

Evaluation and limitations

Use 20 fixed held-out seeds (1000–1019), sampling initial pen position within ±2 mm independently per axis, heading within ±3 degrees, joint positions within ±0.01 rad, and contact friction uniformly from 0.6 to 0.9. Report per-episode values, means, success count, and a binomial confidence interval. These small perturbations test local robustness, not broad generalization.

The human pen differs from the specified object; source metric depth, camera translation, precise transient finger pairs, and pen roll are uncertain. The instruction supplies the requested pair sequence. Simulation success cannot establish real-world transfer, and failures in reconstruction or robot modeling must remain visible alongside any verdict.

Iteration1 training return and survival improve, but accepted pair stages remain zero in the running curves. Two likely causes need testing: wrist exploration is too large for 500Hz impedance control, and the initial robot-specific grasp correction decays before the demonstrated first transfer. Next candidate: smaller wrist action variance and retain the initial correction through the first hold, then taper it during transfer. These are hypotheses, not verified task progress.

decisionFinal-policy design: a closed-loop actor/critic network trained with clipped PPO (Schulman et al., https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.06347). The actor sees noisy joint encoders, wrist state, privileged…

Final-policy design: a closed-loop actor/critic network trained with clipped PPO (Schulman et al., https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.06347). The actor sees noisy joint encoders, wrist state, privileged simulated pen pose/velocity, reference targets, previous actions and phase; it outputs 26 bounded residual commands. The retargeted trajectory is an allowed base controller under LEARNING.md, not the reported policy by itself. No execution-time optimizer, pen attachment or object-pose force is used. Criteria v2 additionally requires pair dominance to exclude a constant multi-finger cage.
